title: Timon of Athens
author: William Shakespeare
setting: Athens, and the woods and shore beyond its walls, in a classical past that is never dated
lengthNote: Around 2,400 lines, which puts it among the shortest of the tragedies
summary: Timon pays a stranger out of a debtors' prison, matches a dowry so that his servant can marry above himself, and hands out jewels and horses to men who thank him in verse. His steward has known for months that the land is sold. When the bills arrive and every friend finds a different form of words for no, Timon calls the same guests back, serves them warm water, drives them out of the house and walks beyond the walls, and spends the last two acts cursing the species from a wood where he has dug up more gold than he ever gave away.

sourceText.label: Project Gutenberg text of the Complete Works of William Shakespeare (eBook 100)
sourceText.note: Every quotation was checked word for word against this text, and act, scene and line references follow the traditional Globe numbering, which modern editions vary from by a line or two.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: The verse and the vocabulary sit close to King Lear. No payment, performance or entry in the Stationers' Register fixes the date.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: Folio only, set between Romeo and Juliet and Julius Caesar in a gap that opened when the printers ran into difficulty over Troilus and Cressida.

atAGlance.label: Co-author
atAGlance.note: Most editors now give him the masque of Cupid and Amazons and much of Act III, including the three refusals. Not everyone is convinced.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Act III is six short scenes in which one request is made and refused three times over.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: The open house
structure.summary: Athens comes to Timon's door with things to sell and favours to ask. He pays five talents to free Ventidius, matches an old man's dowry so that a servant may marry his daughter, and takes a jewel and a painting for which he gives back more than either is worth. At the banquet Apemantus eats a root at his own table and tells the room they are eating their host. Flavius, holding the bills, asks twice for a word and is twice put off.

scenes.title: Fortune's hill
scenes.summary: The Poet, Painter, Jeweller and Merchant wait in the hall and price their wares. The Poet describes his new piece: Fortune throned on a hill, one man beckoned up past his fellows, and every follower letting him slip when she spurns him down.

scenes.title: The petitioners
scenes.summary: Timon frees Ventidius from a debtors' prison, counterpoises a dowry so that Lucilius may marry an old man's daughter, and buys both the painting and the jewel. Apemantus arrives and calls the whole room knaves on the grounds that they are Athenians.

scenes.title: The first banquet
scenes.summary: Ventidius, newly rich, offers to repay the five talents and Timon refuses them. Apemantus takes a table by himself, says a grace that asks the gods for nothing, and watches the guests dip their meat in one man's blood.

scenes.title: The masque and the casket
scenes.summary: Cupid brings in a masque of Amazons with lutes; Timon sends Flavius for the jewels and gives them away with horses and a courser a guest happened to praise. Flavius, aside, works out that his master now owes for every word he speaks.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: The bills come in
structure.summary: A senator does the arithmetic Timon has never done and sends his man out with the bonds. Creditors' servants collect at the gate while dinner goes on inside. Flavius gets his hour at last and lays the books open: the land is sold, the coffers are empty, and the greatest of Timon's having lacks a half of what he owes. Timon's answer is that his wants are a blessing, because now he can find out who his friends are.

scenes.title: The senator counts
scenes.summary: Five-and-twenty thousand owing, and a man who turns a beggar's dog into gold. The senator sends Caphis to Timon's house with the bonds and the dates filled in, and a visage of demand.

scenes.title: Waiting at the gate
scenes.summary: Caphis and the servants of Varro and Isidore press their bills on Timon as he comes in from hunting. He tells them to go to his steward, asks for breath, and walks in to dinner.

scenes.title: Apemantus and the Fool
scenes.summary: While the creditors wait, Apemantus and a brothel-keeper's fool call them usurers' men, asses and bawds between gold and want, and the play stops for a bout of wordplay about fools, knaves and whoremasters.

scenes.title: The accounts
scenes.summary: Flavius shows that he brought the books many times and was waved away. Timon sends servants to Lucius, Lucullus and Sempronius for fifty talents each, and to the senate for a thousand, and is told the senate has already shaken its head.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: Timon’s friends refuse him
structure.summary: Lucullus comes downstairs expecting a present, hears the request and tries to buy the messenger's silence with three coins. Lucius performs astonishment at Lucullus's meanness and then refuses in the same breath. Sempronius, asked fourth, is insulted, not ashamed, that he was not asked first. In the same act the senate condemns a soldier and banishes Alcibiades for pleading mercy, and Timon invites the whole circle back for a second dinner.

scenes.title: Lucullus and the three solidares
scenes.summary: Flaminius is welcomed as the bearer of a gift. When the box under his cloak turns out to be empty, Lucullus explains that friendship is no security for a loan and offers him coins to say he saw nobody. Flaminius throws the money back.

scenes.title: Lucius and Sempronius
scenes.summary: Lucius tells three strangers how little honour Lucullus showed, and then discovers that he unluckily spent everything the day before. Sempronius makes a grievance of the order of asking and sends Timon’s servant away with a couplet about honour and coin.

scenes.title: The bills at the door
scenes.summary: Titus, Hortensius, Philotus and the servants of Varro compare sums in Timon's hall, several of them collecting for lords who are still wearing his jewels. Timon breaks out among them and tells them to cut his heart into sums.

scenes.title: The senate banishes Alcibiades
scenes.summary: Alcibiades asks the senate to spare a soldier who killed a man in hot blood. The senators answer that to bear is valour and to revenge is none, sentence the man to die, and banish Alcibiades for pressing them twice.

scenes.title: Smoke and lukewarm water
scenes.summary: The guests come back, telling one another that the first request must have been a trial of their friendship. Timon says a grace asking the gods to bless nobody, uncovers the dishes, throws the water in their faces and beats them out of the room.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: Out of Athens
structure.summary: Timon turns at the wall and curses the city by rank and by age — matrons, children, bound servants, bankrupts, sons of sixteen — then goes to the woods to live on roots. The household breaks up behind him and Flavius divides the last of his own money among the dismissed servants. Digging for food, Timon turns up gold, and everyone who hears of it comes out to the wood: a general, two women, a philosopher, three thieves, and the one man who followed him for nothing.

scenes.title: The curse at the wall
scenes.summary: Alone outside Athens, Timon asks that obedience fail in children, that bound servants steal and that the wrinkled senate be pulled from the bench, and prays that his own hatred may grow as he grows.

scenes.title: The household breaks up
scenes.summary: The servants ask where their master is. Flavius calls them broken implements of a ruined house, shares out what money he has left among them, and sets off to find Timon and serve him still.

scenes.title: Roots and gold
scenes.summary: Timon digs for a root and turns up gold, and names straight away what it will do: make black white, foul fair and the coward valiant. A drum sounds in the distance and he buries most of it, keeping some out for earnest.

scenes.title: The general and the two women
scenes.summary: Alcibiades arrives with drum and fife on his way to Athens. Timon gives him gold for the war and tells him to spare neither age nor virgin nor babe, then pays Phrynia and Timandra to carry disease back into the city.

scenes.title: Apemantus, the thieves and the steward
scenes.summary: Apemantus accuses Timon of taking up misanthropy only when the money ran out, and they trade insults until a stone is thrown. Three bandits get gold and a lecture proving the sun and moon are thieves. Flavius arrives, weeps, and is named the one honest man alive.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: The tomb and the gate
structure.summary: The Poet and the Painter come out to the cave with promises instead of work, having heard about the gold, and are driven off with what they came for. Two senators offer Timon absolute power in Athens if he will hold Alcibiades off; he offers them his tree to hang themselves on. He dies offstage by the sea, leaving an epitaph that curses whoever reads it, and Alcibiades takes the city on terms.

scenes.title: Promising is the very air o' th' time
scenes.summary: The Poet and the Painter agree to offer Timon a piece each will only promise. He overhears the plan, calls them honest men until the word is worn through, and gives them gold on condition that each drives the other's villain out of his company.

scenes.title: The senators at the cave
scenes.summary: Athens offers Timon the captainship, special dignities and heaps of love and wealth. He says he is writing his epitaph, invites the whole city in order of degree to come and hang on his tree before he fells it, and goes back inside.

scenes.title: Before the walls
scenes.summary: Two more senators hear from a messenger that Alcibiades' files are as full as the report said, and that letters of entreaty have already gone from him to Timon's cave.

scenes.title: The soldier and the wax
scenes.summary: A soldier finds a grave on the sea's edge and an inscription he cannot read, takes the characters away in wax, and carries them to a captain who has skill in every figure.

scenes.title: Alcibiades at the gates
scenes.summary: The senators argue that crimes are not inherited and that the walls were not built by the men who wronged him. Alcibiades throws down his glove, names only his enemies and Timon's for punishment, hears the epitaph read aloud, and marches in.

characters.name: Timon
characters.role: A rich Athenian, afterwards a hermit in the woods
characters.summary: He gives without keeping accounts and believes the giving has bought him a circle of brothers. The belief is put to the test three times in one act and fails three times, after which he cannot revise it by degrees. The same appetite for absolutes that had him dealing kingdoms to his friends has him wishing leprosy on every Athenian, and it never softens, not even for the steward he calls honest.
characters.clue: He frees a stranger from a debtors' prison in his first scene, serves his friends warm water at his last dinner, and digs his own grave at the edge of the sea.

characters.name: Flavius
characters.summary: He keeps the books nobody will open and weeps over them in a back room while the house blazes with lights. The play gives him the two things it treats as unmixed: the scene where he shares his own last money among the servants being turned off, and the scene in the wood where he offers to serve a man who can pay him nothing. Timon's answer is to hand him gold on condition that he hate everybody with it.
characters.clue: He holds the bills through an entire banquet without getting a word in, and later gives his own last coins to the servants being dismissed.

relationships.label: steward to
warns of the same ruin, and is heard as little

characters.name: Apemantus
characters.summary: He comes to the first banquet in order to be thrown out of it, eats a root at a table of his own and tells the room they are eating their host. He is right about everything and it costs him nothing, which is the charge Timon brings against him in the wood: a man bred to nothing has never had anything taken away and cannot be disappointed by anyone.
characters.clue: He says a grace asking the gods for no man but himself, and eats a root while the rest of the table eats its host.

characters.name: Alcibiades
characters.summary: He asks the senate to spare a soldier who killed a man in anger, and is banished for pressing the point twice. He takes Timon's gold, marches on Athens, and then does the thing Timon cannot: he separates the men who wronged him from the city they live in, and enters on terms he sets himself and keeps.
characters.clue: Banished for asking mercy for a friend, he comes back with an army and a glove, and spares everybody he was not sent to punish.

relationships.label: guest of, and funded by him in the wood

characters.name: Lucullus
characters.role: A lord of Athens, and the first friend asked
characters.summary: He comes downstairs expecting a silver basin and ewer, having dreamt of one the night before. Told that the box is empty and the request is for fifty talents, he explains that he has often dined with Timon on purpose to advise him to spend less, and offers Flaminius three small coins to wink at him and say he saw nobody.
characters.clue: He dreamt of silver plate the night before, and offers the messenger three coins to forget the visit.

relationships.label: dined at his table for years, then refused him
first of three refusals in three scenes

characters.name: Lucius
characters.role: A lord of Athens, and the second friend asked
characters.summary: He is telling three visitors how shameful Lucullus has been when Timon's servant arrives at his elbow. Within twenty lines he has remembered a purchase made the day before that leaves him nothing, calls himself a beast for it, and asks the servant to carry his own words back so that the refusal will reach Timon sounding handsome.
characters.clue: He calls another man's refusal dishonourable and then refuses in the next speech, asking for his exact phrases to be repeated.

characters.name: Sempronius
characters.role: A lord of Athens, and the last friend asked
characters.summary: Told that the others have already said no, he is affronted, not ashamed: he was the first man who ever took a gift from Timon and should have been approached first. The refusal comes dressed as injured honour, and the servant left alone on stage calls it a goodly villainy and a man striving hard to appear foul.
characters.clue: He refuses because he was asked fourth, and sends back a rhyme about honour and coin.

relationships.label: first to take a gift from him, last to be asked
the refusal he improves on

characters.name: Ventidius
characters.role: An Athenian whom Timon frees from a debtors' prison
characters.summary: Five talents buy him out before the first scene is over. At the banquet his father has died rich and he offers the money back, and Timon refuses it on the principle that a man who takes payment has not given anything. In Act III, Sempronius mentions in passing that Ventidius has denied him, and he is never seen or spoken of again.
characters.clue: Timon pays five talents to free him and then refuses the repayment; the play mentions his refusal once, in another man's excuse.

relationships.label: freed from prison by him, and silent when asked

characters.name: The Poet
characters.role: A poet with a piece to sell
characters.summary: His new work shows Fortune throned on a hill and the followers who let a man slip when she spurns him down, which is the plot of the play he is standing in. He presents it to the man it is about, takes his money, and in Act V walks out to the cave with nothing in his hands but an intent that is coming toward Timon.
characters.clue: He writes the play's own plot as a poem in the first scene and sells it to its subject.

characters.name: The Painter
characters.role: A painter with a piece to sell
characters.summary: He says a thousand moral paintings could show Fortune's quick blows more plainly than any poem, and then sells Timon a portrait. In the wood he explains that promising is the very air of the time and that performance is a kind of will or testament, and offers an excellent piece he has not started.
characters.clue: He promises an excellent piece he has not painted, having just explained that promising is what the age prefers to doing.

themes.name: Money
themes.summary: Talents, solidares, crowns, bonds, interest, dowries, jewels and horses are counted out all through the play, and every relationship in it has a figure attached. The gold Timon finds in the wood does openly what his generosity did quietly: it brings people to him.
themes.development: In Act I gifts are a currency of love; Act III prices that love at fifty talents and finds it will not pay; in Act IV the metal is dug out of the ground and Timon names its powers one by one.

themes.name: Friendship
themes.summary: Timon's word for the men at his table is brothers, and he tells them the gods provided friends so that he might have need of them. The play then makes him need them, three times in three scenes, and gives each refusal a different set of manners and the same answer.
themes.development: 'I am wealthy in my friends' at the end of Act II is answered by Lucullus, Lucius and Sempronius in Act III, and again by the crowd who come back for a second dinner.

themes.name: Loyal service
themes.summary: The servants keep the play honest. Flaminius throws Lucullus's coins on the floor and curses the meat his master paid for, Flavius brings the accounts and is waved off twice in one scene, and the dismissed household leaves with the steward's own money in their hands.
themes.development: Flavius is interrupted in 1.2, heard at last in 2.2, shares out his wealth in 4.2, and is the single exception Timon allows himself in the wood.

themes.name: Law, mercy and the senate
themes.summary: Alcibiades asks the senate to weigh a soldier's service at Lacedaemon and Byzantium against one killing in hot blood, and is told that to bear is valour and to revenge is none. The same body lends at large interest, refuses Timon a loan, and at the end pleads that crimes are not inherited.
themes.development: The senators freeze Flavius into silence in 2.2, condemn the soldier and banish Alcibiades in 3.5, and in 5.4 ask for exactly the discrimination they would not give.

themes.name: Ceremony
themes.summary: Timon says ceremony was devised to set a gloss on faint deeds and hollow welcomes, and then holds two banquets. The second uses the entire form of hospitality — invitation, music, grace, covered dishes, servants — to serve nothing at all.
themes.development: The masque of Cupid and Amazons in 1.2 is an entertainment Timon pays for and then thanks his guests for; 3.6 repeats the same ceremony with warm water under the covers.

themes.name: Exile
themes.summary: Timon leaves Athens with nothing but nakedness and asks the earth for a root, and the wood immediately fills up with the people he left behind. He has a cave, a spade, a stone to throw, and a grave he chooses himself at the edge of the sea.
themes.development: The curse at the wall in 4.1 promises solitude; 4.3 brings a general, two women, a philosopher, three thieves and a steward; 5.1 brings the senators and the two artists.

themes.name: Warnings ignored
themes.summary: Everybody in the play can state its moral. The Poet has written it as an allegory, Apemantus says it at the table, Flavius works it out in the corner with the bills in his hand, and Timon hears all three and goes on giving until there is nothing left to give.
themes.development: The Fortune speech of 1.1 forecasts the fall, the asides of 1.2 count what it will cost, the fall arrives in 3.4, and Timon concludes that mankind is vile, not merely that he misjudged some men.

techniques.name: Catalogue
techniques.definition: A list allowed to run on past the point of usefulness, so that the accumulation itself becomes the effect.
techniques.inThisBook: The curse at the wall in 4.1 works through Athenian society in order — matrons, children, slaves, bankrupts, bound servants, sons of sixteen — and the instructions to Alcibiades go through honoured age, matron, virgin and babe. The lists get longer as the argument gets weaker.

techniques.name: Antithesis
techniques.definition: Two opposites set against each other inside a single line, so that the sentence turns on the join.
techniques.inThisBook: The gold speech is built of pairs: black white, foul fair, wrong right, base noble, old young, coward valiant. Six reversals in two lines with no verb between them, which is the whole claim about what money does.

techniques.name: Epigram
techniques.definition: A short balanced sentence that sounds like settled wisdom and usually turns a received idea inside out.
techniques.inThisBook: Scene after scene closes on a rhyming couplet that settles the argument: 'Who bates mine honour shall not know my coin', 'Feast-won, fast-lost', 'Men shut their doors against a setting sun'. Self-interest keeps arriving in the shape of a proverb.

techniques.name: The set piece
techniques.definition: A self-contained episode built to a single effect and complete in itself, whether comic or ceremonial.
techniques.inThisBook: Both banquets are complete performances, and the second is an exact copy of the first with the food taken out. The masque of Cupid and Amazons in 1.2 is a court entertainment dropped whole into the middle of a dinner and applauded by the man paying for it.

techniques.name: Stage property
techniques.definition: An object handled on stage that carries far more weight than its use in the scene explains.
techniques.inThisBook: A casket of jewels, an empty box under Flaminius's cloak, three solidares thrown on the floor, a sheaf of bills, covered dishes, a spade, a root, a stone, a glove and a wax impression of an epitaph. The argument is carried by things passing from hand to hand.

techniques.name: Double plot
techniques.definition: A second story running beside the first, repeating its problem in another key and commenting on it.
techniques.inThisBook: Alcibiades is wronged by Athens in the same act as Timon, exiled in the same act, and given gold in the same scene in the wood. He is the control in the experiment: the same injury, and a man who can still tell one Athenian from another.

techniques.name: Foils
techniques.definition: A character constructed to throw another's choices into relief by making different ones.
techniques.inThisBook: Apemantus has hated mankind from the start and it has never cost him anything; Flavius has every reason to hate and does not. Timon stands between them, and the long quarrel of 4.3 is an argument about which of the two he has turned into.

quotations.text: When Fortune in her shift and change of mood Spurns down her late beloved, all his dependants, Which laboured after him to the mountain's top Even on their knees and hands, let him slip down, Not one accompanying his declining foot.
quotations.speaker: Poet
quotations.context: Describing to the Painter the poem he has brought to the house to sell.
quotations.analysis: The Poet summarises the next four acts before any of them have happened, then hands the manuscript to the man who will fall. 'Let him slip down' is the exact verb: nobody pushes, everyone simply stops holding on. The scene offers no clean division between corrupt flatterers and honest art, because the diagnosis is itself for sale.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, The Life of Timon of Athens, 1.1.84-88

quotations.text: I gave it freely ever, and there's none Can truly say he gives if he receives.
quotations.speaker: Timon
quotations.context: Refusing the five talents Ventidius has come to the banquet to repay.
quotations.analysis: Good ethics and ruinous accounting. By defining a gift as something that cannot be handed back, Timon puts every friend permanently in his debt and forbids them to clear it. That is precisely the position they use against him in Act III, when there is nothing written anywhere that says they owe him a talent.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, The Life of Timon of Athens, 1.2.10-11

quotations.text: O you gods, what a number of men eats Timon, and he sees 'em not! It grieves me to see so many dip their meat in one man's blood
quotations.speaker: Apemantus
quotations.context: At his own table at the first banquet, refusing Timon's food.
quotations.analysis: In Apemantus’s line the dinner becomes cannibalism with one verb: the guests do not eat with Timon, they eat Timon. It is the play's governing image of consumption and it is literally true of the estate, which the guests are working through course by course. He says it aloud, at the table, in front of everyone, and nothing whatever follows.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, The Life of Timon of Athens, 1.2.39-42

quotations.text: I should fear those that dance before me now Would one day stamp upon me. 'T has been done. Men shut their doors against a setting sun.
quotations.speaker: Apemantus
quotations.context: Watching the masque of Amazons that Cupid has brought into the banquet.
quotations.analysis: The couplet has the shape of a proverb and the function of a prophecy: in 3.4 Timon finds his own doors shut against him from the inside. 'Stamp' keeps the dancing in view, so that the feet entertaining him now are the feet that will be on him, and the line is spoken over music nobody else stops hearing.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, The Life of Timon of Athens, 1.2.141-143

quotations.text: His promises fly so beyond his state That what he speaks is all in debt; he owes For every word.
quotations.speaker: Flavius
quotations.context: Aside, while Timon sends out for the casket of jewels.
quotations.analysis: Flavius makes speech itself a form of borrowing. Timon's generosity is verbal before it is financial — he gives away the bay courser because a guest praised it in passing — so every sentence draws on an account already empty. It is the most precise thing said about him in the play, and it is said to nobody at all.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, The Life of Timon of Athens, 1.2.196-198

quotations.text: If I want gold, steal but a beggar's dog And give it Timon, why, the dog coins gold.
quotations.speaker: A Senator
quotations.context: Going through his ledger at home, and deciding to call in what Timon owes.
quotations.analysis: The senator has found the mechanism and states it as a recipe: worthless object in, gold out. His is the first voice to treat Timon's bounty as a market and not a virtue, and the calculation ends with an order to fetch the bonds and fill in the dates. Athens does not set out to ruin Timon; it simply notices him.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, The Life of Timon of Athens, 2.1.5-6

quotations.text: Ah, when the means are gone that buy this praise, The breath is gone whereof this praise is made. Feast-won, fast-lost
quotations.speaker: Flavius
quotations.context: Laying the accounts before Timon at last, after the creditors have been sent from the door.
quotations.analysis: Praise is made of breath and paid for with dinners, so when the dinners stop the praise simply evaporates; the metaphor is physical, not moral. 'Feast-won, fast-lost' compresses the whole of Act III into four words, and the two senses of fast — quickly, and going without food — sit one on top of the other.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, The Life of Timon of Athens, 2.2.178-180

quotations.text: For by these Shall I try friends. You shall perceive how you Mistake my fortunes. I am wealthy in my friends.
quotations.speaker: Timon
quotations.context: Answering Flavius, who has just shown him that the land is sold and the debts unpayable.
quotations.analysis: He has been told he is ruined and he hears an opportunity. 'Try' means test, and he is right that a test is coming; what he has wrong is which way it will go. The line is the hinge of the play, and the confidence in it is why the three refusals of Act III land as hard as they do.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, The Life of Timon of Athens, 2.2.185-187

quotations.text: this is no time to lend money, especially upon bare friendship without security. Here's three solidares for thee. Good boy, wink at me, and say thou saw'st me not.
quotations.speaker: Lucullus
quotations.context: To Flaminius, who has come with an empty box to ask for fifty talents.
quotations.analysis: 'Bare friendship' is the entire refusal in two words: friendship stripped of collateral is not a thing a man lends against. Lucullus then tries to buy a servant's eyesight for three small coins, which is the rate he puts on a house he has dined in for years. Flaminius throws them on the floor and curses the meat in him.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, The Life of Timon of Athens, 3.1.42-46

quotations.text: But I perceive Men must learn now with pity to dispense, For policy sits above conscience.
quotations.speaker: First Stranger
quotations.context: After watching Lucius refuse the servant, having just heard him call Lucullus shameful for doing the same.
quotations.analysis: The verdict is given to a man with nothing at stake — he says he never tasted Timon in his life — which is what makes it a judgement on Athens and not a grievance. To dispense with something is to do without it. Pity has become an optional expense, and the strangers are watching a city decide it can no longer afford one.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, The Life of Timon of Athens, 3.2.89-91

quotations.text: And with their faint reply this answer join: Who bates mine honour shall not know my coin.
quotations.speaker: Sempronius
quotations.context: Refusing the fourth request, after being told that Lucullus, Lucius and Ventidius have all said no.
quotations.analysis: Sempronius is the only one who does not trouble to sound sorry. Being asked last is the injury; the money is incidental to it. 'Bates' means lessens, and by rhyming honour against coin he states the exchange rate he is working to. The servant, left alone, calls it a man striving hard to appear foul, which will do for the whole act.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, The Life of Timon of Athens, 3.3.28-29

quotations.text: Knock me down with 'em! Cleave me to the girdle. … Cut my heart in sums! … Tell out my blood.
quotations.speaker: Timon
quotations.context: Breaking out of his own house among the creditors' servants and their bills.
quotations.analysis: Three short answers to three bills, and in each a sum becomes an injury to the body. ‘Tell out’ means count out, so blood is being reckoned in the units that money is reckoned in: the metaphor the play has been building since the first banquet is finally spoken by the man it is about. Within twenty lines he has ordered another dinner.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, The Life of Timon of Athens, 3.4.89-96

quotations.text: Banish me? Banish your dotage, banish usury, That makes the Senate ugly.
quotations.speaker: Alcibiades
quotations.context: Sentenced to exile for pressing the senate a second time to spare a soldier's life.
quotations.analysis: He takes their verb and turns it three times, and the third turn names what is actually wrong with the room: the men refusing mercy are lending at large interest. It is the same charge the Timon plot brings against Athens, said out loud in the senate house, and it gets him thrown out of the city instead of answered.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, The Life of Timon of Athens, 3.5.97-99

quotations.text: May you a better feast never behold, You knot of mouth-friends! Smoke and lukewarm water Is your perfection.
quotations.speaker: Timon
quotations.context: Uncovering the dishes at the second banquet.
quotations.analysis: 'Mouth-friends' is the play's best coinage: friends who exist at a table and no further than the mouth. Warm water is what a feast leaves when the food is taken out of it, the honest substance under the sauces, and 'perfection' means completion — the finished form of what they always were. He then throws it in their faces.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, The Life of Timon of Athens, 3.6.89-92

quotations.text: Timon will to the woods, where he shall find Th' unkindest beast more kinder than mankind.
quotations.speaker: Timon
quotations.context: Turning at the city wall for a last look before leaving Athens.
quotations.analysis: He speaks of himself in the third person, as though reading his own epitaph early. The play on kind — a species, and kindness — carries the argument: the beast is kinder because it was never of his kind. Apemantus takes the comparison apart in 4.3 by showing that every beast in the list is prey to some other beast.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, The Life of Timon of Athens, 4.1.35-36

quotations.text: Poor honest lord, brought low by his own heart, Undone by goodness! Strange, unusual blood When man's worst sin is he does too much good!
quotations.speaker: Flavius
quotations.context: Alone, after dividing his own last money among the dismissed servants.
quotations.analysis: This is the most generous reading of Timon in the play and it comes from the one man entitled to be bitter about him. 'Blood' here means temperament. Flavius does not claim the giving was wise, only that the fault in it was goodness, and the exclamation marks are the sound of a bookkeeper running out of categories.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, The Life of Timon of Athens, 4.2.37-40

quotations.text: Thus much of this will make Black white, foul fair, wrong right, Base noble, old young, coward valiant.
quotations.speaker: Timon
quotations.context: Digging for a root outside his cave, and turning up gold instead.
quotations.analysis: Six reversals in two lines with no verbs between them, so that the transformations happen as fast as the words are said. Gold is not being called evil here; it is being called a translator, able to exchange any value for its opposite. Marx quoted the speech in 1844 and again in Capital for exactly that claim about money.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, The Life of Timon of Athens, 4.3.28-30

quotations.text: This yellow slave Will knit and break religions, bless th' accursed, Make the hoar leprosy adored, place thieves And give them title, knee, and approbation With senators on the bench.
quotations.speaker: Timon
quotations.context: The same speech, a few lines on, with the gold in his hands.
quotations.analysis: Calling gold a slave and then listing what it commands is the joke inside the image: the thing that serves is the thing that rules. 'Knee' and 'approbation' were the currency of Act I, when the lobbies filled with tendance, and here the same bowing is bought openly. He buries most of the gold and keeps out enough to go on proving the point.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, The Life of Timon of Athens, 4.3.34-39

quotations.text: The middle of humanity thou never knewest, but the extremity of both ends.
quotations.speaker: Apemantus
quotations.context: In the wood, in the middle of the insult match that ends with a stone being thrown.
quotations.analysis: The sharpest criticism of Timon in the play, and the reason it is hard to call him a tragic hero: there is no scene in which he learns anything, only a switch from one absolute to its opposite. Apemantus has earned the observation by occupying the same extreme for years and knowing exactly what it is worth.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, The Life of Timon of Athens, 4.3.300-301

quotations.text: The sun's a thief and with his great attraction Robs the vast sea; the moon's an arrant thief, And her pale fire she snatches from the sun
quotations.speaker: Timon
quotations.context: Giving gold to three bandits, and proving to them that theft is universal.
quotations.analysis: A piece of real natural philosophy — evaporation, reflected light, the tides — recruited to tell three robbers that nothing they do is exceptional. It talks one of them out of the trade, which is the last thing Timon wants; he means to make them worse. Nabokov took the title of a novel from the phrase in the third line.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, The Life of Timon of Athens, 4.3.439-441

quotations.text: I do proclaim One honest man, mistake me not, but one; No more, I pray, and he's a steward.
quotations.speaker: Timon
quotations.context: To Flavius, who has found him in the wood and wept at the sight of him.
quotations.analysis: The concession is fenced on both sides — 'but one', 'no more, I pray' — because a second honest man would wreck the argument he has built his exile on. That the one should be a steward, a paid servant with no reason left to stay, is the quietest rebuke in the play to everything Timon believed about brothers commanding one another's fortunes.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, The Life of Timon of Athens, 4.3.500-502

quotations.text: Why, I was writing of my epitaph; It will be seen tomorrow. My long sickness Of health and living now begins to mend And nothing brings me all things.
quotations.speaker: Timon
quotations.context: Refusing the senators who have come to the cave to offer him command of Athens.
quotations.analysis: Health and living are the disease and dying is the cure, and the inversion is held perfectly steady across three lines. 'Nothing brings me all things' is the last of his reversals and the calmest of them: he has stopped cursing and started arranging. It is also the only preparation the play gives for a death that happens offstage.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, The Life of Timon of Athens, 5.1.185-188

quotations.text: Here lies a wretched corse, of wretched soul bereft. Seek not my name. A plague consume you, wicked caitiffs left! Here lie I, Timon, who alive all living men did hate. Pass by and curse thy fill, but pass and stay not here thy gait.
quotations.speaker: Alcibiades
quotations.context: Reading aloud at the gates from the wax impression a soldier has taken off the tomb by the sea.
quotations.analysis: Two epitaphs printed as one, contradicting each other inside four lines: the first forbids you to seek his name and the second gives it. Both stand in North's Plutarch as separate inscriptions, one said to be Timon's own and one by the poet Callimachus. The collision has been read as a sign of unfinished work and as a last joke by a man who could not stop giving.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, The Life of Timon of Athens, 5.4.70-73

quotations.text: Bring me into your city, And I will use the olive with my sword, Make war breed peace, make peace stint war, make each Prescribe to other, as each other's leech.
quotations.speaker: Alcibiades
quotations.context: The last speech of the play, immediately after the epitaph has been read out at the walls.
quotations.analysis: The play ends with the one man who can tell one Athenian from another. 'Leech' means physician, so war and peace are set to treat each other, and the balanced clauses do on the page what the terms do in the city. It is a settlement and not a reconciliation: nobody is forgiven, and the cure is mutual restraint.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, The Life of Timon of Athens, 5.4.81-84

timeline.label: North's Plutarch published in English
timeline.detail: The Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romanes, where the lives of Antony and Alcibiades carry the few paragraphs about Timon and both of the epitaphs.

timeline.label: An academic Timon comedy circulates in manuscript
timeline.detail: An anonymous English play on the same story, with a mock banquet of painted stones, survives from about this date. Whether Shakespeare knew it is disputed.

timeline.label: The play written, probably with Thomas Middleton
timeline.detail: No payment, performance or Stationers' Register entry fixes the date. The verse and the vocabulary sit close to King Lear.

timeline.label: Printed in the First Folio
timeline.detail: The only early text, set between Romeo and Juliet and Julius Caesar in a gap that opened when the printers ran into difficulty over Troilus and Cressida.

timeline.label: Shadwell's The History of Timon of Athens, the Man-Hater
timeline.detail: An adaptation that gave Timon two women, one faithful and one false, and kept the story on the London stage for most of a century.

timeline.label: Richard Cumberland's version at Drury Lane
timeline.detail: Another rewriting, this time providing Timon with a daughter to be married to Alcibiades.

timeline.label: Samuel Phelps stages it at Sadler's Wells
timeline.detail: Close to Shakespeare's text, and the first London production in generations that was not an adaptation.

timeline.label: Paul Scofield plays Timon for the Royal Shakespeare Company
timeline.detail: Directed by John Schlesinger at Stratford, and the production that brought the play back into the regular repertory.

timeline.label: Richard Pasco plays Timon for the RSC
timeline.detail: One of a run of postwar revivals that treated the play as a study of patronage and money instead of an unfinished curiosity.

timeline.label: Gregory Doran directs Michael Pennington at the RSC
timeline.detail: Staged in a world of corporate hospitality, with the first banquet played as a company party.

timeline.label: The New Oxford Shakespeare prints it as a collaboration
timeline.detail: Timon of Athens appears under two names, Shakespeare's and Middleton's, after decades of stylistic and textual work.

timeline.label: Simon Godwin directs Kathryn Hunter as Timon
timeline.detail: At the RSC, with gold as the visible substance of the first half and a set that decayed as the money went.

places.note: Plutarch's town. His lives of Antony and Alcibiades hold the few paragraphs the play grew from, and both epitaphs.

criticalViews.summary: Abrupt joins, duplicated functions, uneven verse and a cluster of spellings and favourite words that are Middleton's have persuaded most editors that he wrote the masque in the first banquet and much of Act III, including the three refusals.
criticalViews.counter: The evidence is statistical and the samples are small. Some scholars hold that one author writing fast, or revising and then leaving the job, would produce much the same traces.

criticalViews.position: The play as an unfinished draft
criticalViews.summary: The loose ends support it: the sums Timon owes do not agree from one scene to the next, a Fool arrives with Apemantus and is never accounted for, and some of the Folio's directions read like notes an author was still working from.
criticalViews.counter: The same features work in performance. A world that goes from crowded luxury to an empty wood does not need consistent bookkeeping, and productions since 1965 have found the breaks useful, not awkward.

criticalViews.summary: Timon shows gold doing openly what patronage does quietly: turning one kind of value into another. Marx read the speech on black and white, foul and fair as a description of money's power to make contradictory things exchangeable, and quoted it twice.
criticalViews.counter: The economics are a rich man's. Timon never works, never trades and finds his gold lying in the ground, so the play can say a great deal about credit and nothing at all about where wealth comes from.

essayQuestions.question: Is Timon generous?
essayQuestions.focus: Giving, obligation, and what the gifts are for
plan: Start with what he actually gives in Act I: five talents for Ventidius, a dowry matched to an old man's, a jewel, a bay courser handed over because a guest praised it.
Take his refusal of Ventidius's repayment at 1.2.10 seriously as a principle, then ask what it does to people who are never allowed to discharge the debt.
Use Flavius's aside at 1.2.196 to show that the giving was already borrowing, and that the steward was never permitted to say so out loud.
Weigh Apemantus's charge that a man who loves flattery deserves the flatterer against the fact that Timon gives to a soldier, a servant and a prisoner as well as to lords.
Close on 'I am wealthy in my friends' and decide whether the gifts were a reasonable hope of return or a demand that was never stated.

essayQuestions.question: What does Act III achieve by refusing Timon three times over?
essayQuestions.focus: Repetition, variation and the making of a society
plan: Set the three scenes out as a sequence: Lucullus with a bribe, Lucius with an alibi, Sempronius with a grievance about being asked last.
Notice that each refusal closes on a rhymed couplet, so that self-interest keeps arriving in the voice of proverbial wisdom.
Bring in the three Strangers of 3.2, who have taken nothing from Timon and deliver the judgement the characters will not.
Put the banishment of Alcibiades in 3.5 beside the refusals, and show the senate doing the same thing on a public scale.
Ask what the second banquet of 3.6 adds that the three scenes have not already proved.

essayQuestions.question: 'The middle of humanity thou never knewest.' How fair is Apemantus's account of Timon?
essayQuestions.focus: Misanthropy, cost, and the limits of self-knowledge
plan: Establish Apemantus's position in Act I: at the table, eating a root, describing exactly what is happening and changing nothing by it.
Examine Timon's counter-charge in 4.3 that a man bred in sufferance has never had anything taken from him and has nothing to give up.
Test the claim that Timon reaches no middle by tracing Act IV, where the curses grow longer as the argument behind them gets thinner.
Set Flavius against both men: every reason to hate mankind, and no inclination to do it.
Decide whether the play offers any position between the two extremes, or whether Alcibiades's terms at the gates are the only one on offer.

essayQuestions.question: Why does the play give its last scene to Alcibiades?
plan: Line up the two exiles: both wronged by Athens in Act III, both handed gold in the wood, both promising ruin to the city.
Follow what Timon does with his gold in 4.3 — pays for war, disease and theft — and set it against what Alcibiades does with his.
Read the senators' plea in 5.4 that crimes are not inherited, and note that it is the argument Alcibiades made for his soldier in 3.5.
Look closely at the glove, the named offenders, and the promise that not a man shall pass his quarter.
Weigh the epitaph, read aloud at the gates, against the four lines that follow it, and say what kind of ending the play has chosen.

discussionQuestions: Timon refuses Ventidius's repayment on the grounds that a gift taken back is not a gift. Is he right, and what does the rule cost the people around him?
Everyone in Act I can see what is coming: the Poet has written it, Apemantus says it at the table, Flavius counts it in the corner. Why does no warning land?
The three refusals happen in three scenes with three different excuses. Would the play be stronger or weaker with one?
Timon goes looking for a root and finds gold. Is that a joke, a judgement, or simply bad luck?
Flavius is the one honest man Timon will allow. Does the play agree with him, or is it showing a man narrowing the world all over again?
Timon dies offstage and the last we have of him is a soldier's wax rubbing. What would be lost if we saw him die?

related.why: The other play about a man who gives everything away and then goes out into the weather to find out what he is worth without it.
Written close to it: another ancient city that cannot accommodate its own great man, and another exile who comes back at the head of an army.
Bonds, interest and the question of what friendship is security for, argued in a courtroom instead of across a dinner table.
The same arithmetic from the other end: a man who keeps everything, and what it takes to make him open his hands.
Webster's Bosola serves a court he despises for wages, which is the bargain Apemantus refuses and Flavius keeps without asking for one.
